Safety of Indian seafarers, tankers raised in Doval’s conversation with Iranian counterpart, says MEA

PTI

14 October, 2026 09:47 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

New Delhi, Oct 14 (PTI) The issue of safety and security of Indian seafarers and tankers figured in the recent phone conversation between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday.

The two sides also discussed regional situation and international developments, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in response to a query during his bi-weekly media briefing.

The telephonic conversation that took place on October 12 focused on the prevailing security situation in West Asia.

Show Full Article

Jaiswal was asked the details about the outcome of the conversation, and if India raised the issue of attacks on Indian-flagged vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Regarding the conversation that our National Security Advisor had with his counterpart in Iran, this conversation happened on October 12. National Security Advisor spoke to the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council of Iran, His Excellency Dr Mohsen Rezaei,” he said.

“They discussed bilateral issues. They also discussed regional situation and international developments. And during the meeting, the safety and security of Indian seafarers was raised, as the safety and security of Indian tankers was also raised,” Jaiswal added.

New Delhi has maintained that the repeated attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Gulf are “completely unacceptable and must cease immediately”.

India on Wednesday condemned the string of attacks on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, saying the “totally unacceptable” acts need to cease immediately.

New Delhi also asserted that it remains committed to doing the best for the welfare and well-being of Indian nationals abroad.

India has been consistently calling for resolution of the West Asia crisis through dialogue and diplomacy.

New Delhi has also been concerned over spate of attacks on merchant ships in the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz.

When asked about the proposed India-US bilateral trade agreement, Jaiswal said External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has spoken about it at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum. Both sides remain engaged on this particular matter for a mutually beneficial bilateral trade agreement, he said.

India and the US are continuing to engage to iron out differences on the proposed trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a “landing point”, Jaishankar said on Tuesday, while noting that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.

Asked if the H-1B issue and the recent comments made by the US vice president will be raised during US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s upcoming visit to India, Jaiswal just said “several issues of bilateral nature will be discussed”.

Rubio will travel to India next week to further strengthen energy cooperation, the US Department of State said on Tuesday.

Jaiswal was also asked about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s expected visit to Canada, and whether the bilateral trade deal is likely to be concluded before the visit.

On the trade deal, Jaiswal said the fifth round of negotiations happened in Ottawa a week ago or so, and both sides remain committed to a mutually beneficial Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).

PM Modi, after a telephonic conversation with his Canadian counterpart Mark Carney on Tuesday, said he had a “warm and productive” conversation with him and both leaders agreed to build on the “positive momentum” in bilateral ties.

Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand, who is on a working visit to India, on Wednesday met Modi. The PM said they had a productive discussion on further strengthening India-Canada ties in trade, technology and energy.

Asked about the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council raising issues related to recent communal incidents, Jaiswal said, “It is our expectation that such issues will be addressed by the Bangladeshi side.”

On the Home Ministers’ Meeting of BIMSTEC here on Tuesday, the MEA spokesperson said, “We had participation from all BIMSTEC countries, and post the conversation, the meeting, a Delhi Declaration was also adopted, wherein the commitment of all the BIMSTEC countries to strengthen cooperation across a range of areas including fight against terrorism, counter-narcotics measures, and anti-money laundering cooperation.”

“It is our expectation that with this inaugural dialogue, there will be a stronger security cooperation among all members,” he said.

On the recent comment made by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) in Geneva over the recent detention of thousands of protesters in Delhi, he reiterated that it was “unwarranted” and at the same time “unacceptable because it amounts to interference” in India’s internal affairs.

They have, it seems, an approach of “extreme selectivity” and if they continue on this path, then obviously, it will lead to loss of faith in multilateralism, Jaiswal said, adding that at the same time, it “undermines their credibility as an organisation”. PTI KND KVK

China’s funding of global development institutions rises tenfold since 2010 to $3 billion

This makes China the fifth-largest donor to the International Development Association, which is the World Bank’s fund for the poorest countries.

Aakriti Handa

14 October, 2026 07:07 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: China’s funding to development-focussed multilateral institutions increased to more than $3 billion in 2024, registering a ten-fold increase from $260 million in 2010, according to a study conducted by the Center for Global Development.

This makes China the fifth-largest donor to the International Development Association (IDA), which is the World Bank’s fund for the poorest countries, up from the 28th position it held in 2010.

China rose the ranks thanks to its latest pledge of a whopping $1.5 million to the latest replenishment. China’s funding to multilateral development banks or MDBs — that provide grants and loans on favourable terms to poorer countries — has increased by 92% over the past five years. MDBs are funded by multiple countries to finance large development projects that emerging economies may struggle to fund alone.

Show Full Article

The study, authored by Beata Cichocka and Ian Mitchell, also found a sharp increase in China’s multilateral climate-finance footprint, from $600 million in 2017 to $5.25 billion in 2025.

Although China’s contributions to the development-oriented multilaterals have grown more than tenfold since 2010, they remain highly selective. In other words, China is not uniformly amping up funding across various multilateral banks.

China’s contributions to development-oriented multilaterals, 2011–2024 | Screenshot: Center for Global Development study titled ‘China in the Multilateral Development System’ It ranks only 19th for voluntary contributions to the United Nations and contributes to just seven of the 26 vertical funds (like Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance; the Global Fund; or the Green Climate Fund). Its funding is concentrated in MDB concessional windows that provide loans on more generous terms, especially the International Development Association, and in climate finance. Hence, China remains a modest vertical fund donor and a limited voluntary UN funder.

Its overall contributions to vertical funds have fallen by 32 per cent.

More funding; less borrowing At the same time, China is borrowing less from development banks—its borrowing from MDBs has fallen nearly by half, from over $8 billion in 2021 to $4.7 billion in 2024. At the World Bank too, China has plummeted from being the largest borrower in 2017 to only the 18th largest borrower in 2025. In fact, the World Bank estimates that China will stop borrowing altogether after 2031.

China’s borrowing from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), a multilateral development bank it helped establish and is its largest shareholder, has also declined markedly since 2017.

However, China’s growing financial contribution has not led to it becoming more influential at these development banks. China’s voting power has largely remained unchanged since 2021.

Despite holding 6 per cent of the shares in the World Bank, it holds lesser voting power than the around 12 per cent implied by the Bank’s own shareholding formula.

In addition, Chinese nationals now hold fewer top UN jobs than they did five years ago, having lost leadership positions at WHO, ITU, UNIDO and WMO. Chinese nationals lead just two of the 56 development-relevant UN bodies examined and make up only 1.3 percent of the wider UN staff, despite China accounting for around 17 percent of the world’s population.

China is indeed neither withdrawing from the existing multilateral system nor simply replacing traditional Western donors within it. It is becoming more deeply embedded across a range of institutions—notably, the World Bank’s IDA and WHO—while engaging on terms that preserve its flexibility.

India working to rebuild ties with China; open to JVs with any country based on fair deal: Goyal

PTI

14 October, 2026 06:45 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi, Oct 14 (PTI) Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Wednesday said India is working to rebuild its relations with China, but the last word on this journey has not yet been scripted .

He also said India is open to joint ventures with any country, provided it gets a fair deal.

“We are open to all countries around the world as long as we get a fair deal, as long as we ensure a continuity in the engagement, and as long as the geopolitical situation does not deteriorate. I think we had some concerns in the past. We are working to develop relations with China once again, but the last word has not yet been scripted on this journey,” he said addressing the Bloomberg New Economy Forum.

Show Full Article

In the last few months, the two sides have taken a series of measures to rebuild their ties after they came under severe strain following the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020.

On September 12, Prime Minister Narendra Modi conveyed to Chinese President Xi Jinping that peace and tranquillity along the frontier remains “essential” basis for development of India-China relations, even as the two leaders welcomed “steady progress” in the bilateral ties.

The two leaders had met on the sidelines of the BRICS summit here last month.

After over four years of frosty ties over the eastern Ladakh military standoff, the two neighbours began to repair their relations following a meeting between Modi and Xi in the Russian city of Kazan in October 2024 that was held after the face-off ended.

Goyal’s remarks assume importance as China is India’s second-largest trading partner. India has time and again raised concerns over the widening trade deficit with China.

Bilateral trade between the two countries rose 7.9 per cent in 2025-26 to USD 127.7 billion from USD 118.39 billion in 2024-25.

India’s exports to China grew 36.62 per cent to USD 19.47 billion in 2025-26 from USD 14.25 billion a year ago. Imports, on the other hand, rose 16 per cent to USD 131.62 billion during the period. The trade deficit widened to USD 99.19 billion in the last fiscal from USD 85 billion in 2024-25 — an area of concern for the country.

There are also issues related to investments from China as India has tightened its FDI policy for countries sharing land borders with it.

Talking about the current geopolitical challenges, Goyal said “Everybody has recognised the importance of friends, and that’s going to be the most important critical element in the years to come”.

Recalling the Covid period, the minister said India focused on self-sufficiency after a number of countries declined to supply essential items.

While India provided food grains and vaccines to over 100 countries during Covid, “we found that most countries let us down very badly,” he said.

“During Covid, we really recognised the vulnerabilities that a nation like India, a large nation of 1.4 billion people, had to go through when supply chains were broken. We did not get adequate material for meeting our needs during Covid. Wherever we had placed orders for personal protective equipment or Covid kits or vaccines, we were let down miserably by all countries,” he added.

Goyal further said, “When we needed Pfizer and Moderna vaccines, the West refused to give it to us… They even refused to make an application to get the vaccine into the Indian market, even though we were willing to waive all the conditions. So, it’s a global phenomenon.”

In response to that experience, Prime Minister Narendra Modi “gave the clarion call for Atmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliant India),” Goyal said.

Speaking at the Forum, Singapore’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Kim Yong said Singapore and India are in talks to strengthen the semi-conductor industry in India.

“We are also working on training and skilling of the Indian workforce so that we can support the growth of semiconductors,” he added.

India and Singapore trade pact came into force in 2005. PTI RR RR VHI

AI models could soon replicate themselves across smart TVs, fridges, Anthropic warns

Researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman found that AI models can run on unfamiliar hardware and that one tested model achieved end-to-end replication in a simplified environment.

Himanshi Aggarwal

14 October, 2026 06:41 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

OpenAI and Anthropic logos in illustration | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Anthropic researchers have warned that AI models could soon be able to replicate themselves autonomously, even without access to external data centres.

New research from Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team has found that small artificial intelligence models could independently copy themselves across commercial Internet of Things (IoT) devices, such as smart TVs, fridges, vacuum cleaners and ovens.

The findings, published on 12 October and authored by researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, report that models with around 9 billion parameters already show a strong ability to set up and run inference (the process of generating outputs) on a wide range of unfamiliar hardware. By the end of this year, smaller models, too, could achieve full end-to-end self-replication.

Show Full Article

“Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes,” the research paper states.

The research also highlights the risks posed by such replication.

“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days),” the researchers explain. “Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.”

Traditional computer worms copy code from one machine to another. An “AI worm” could carry its own model weights (or re-download them) and then run inference on newly infected hardware. This could result in autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA)—an AI system that deploys and spreads itself without human control.

The research focused on low-powered, poorly secured consumer devices.

In the experiments, smaller models succeeded in setting themselves up and running on a range of different devices. More capable models completed the full cycle more effectively, scanning a network, transferring themselves and launching new copies. Only the most advanced model among those tested achieved consistent end-to-end replication in a simplified environment.

“Only GLM-5.2 out of our set of tested open-weight models is capable of full end-to-end replication,” the paper states.

The researchers estimate that smaller models could reach a similar level of competence by the end of the year. By then, models small enough to run on ordinary IoT hardware could become capable of spreading on their own.

However, the spread is likely to be slow.

“As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days,” the paper states.

While a single replication cycle might take a day or two, a large number of infected devices could support many simultaneous copies of the AI. The resulting network could be comparable in scale to past IoT botnets that compromised millions of devices.

Unlike conventional malware, self-replicating AI malware might be able to figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. Traditional botnets usually target specific types of devices using fixed instructions. In the experiments, success rates improved when later versions of a model inherited notes from earlier attempts.

Anthropic also outlines several possible defences.

Unusual network traffic caused by model transfers and device-to-device communication could be detected by internet service providers. Quarantining infected networks, as was done to contain earlier botnets, has proved effective in the past. Stronger security defaults from device manufacturers, already required in some countries, could also reduce the pool of vulnerable targets.

“The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication,” the researchers conclude. “Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain.”

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)
